idiom_name: mutex-protected correlation table + pthread_cond_timedwait reply wait
implementation_notes: C has no request/reply runtime, so the requestor hand-writes the classic structure: a correlation table (request id -> waiter) guarded by a mutex, an atomically incremented request id carried in the request envelope, and a bounded wait for the reply with pthread_cond_timedwait - or mq_timedreceive, poll, or a socket read with SO_RCVTIMEO. The replier copies the id from the request into the reply and signals the matching waiter; on ETIMEDOUT the entry is removed and the caller gets a deadline error. libzmq's REQ/REP sockets (or the nng/nanomsg equivalents) replace the hand-built table when a messaging library is acceptable, because REQ/REP moves correlation into the socket pair.
pitfalls: pthread_cond_timedwait takes an absolute timespec and defaults to the CLOCK_REALTIME condvar clock: set CLOCK_MONOTONIC with pthread_condattr_setclock or a clock adjustment can expire - or silently extend - the wait.

The waiter is owned by the caller's stack frame, so a late reply must never write into an entry that already timed out and was removed; refcount the waiter or key replies by generation to avoid use-after-free.

One shared reply descriptor read by several threads needs a single demultiplexer thread that looks the id up and signals the right waiter; letting each thread read the socket hands replies to the wrong requester.

variants.name: ZeroMQ REQ/REP sockets with a poll timeout
variants.idiom_name: libzmq REQ/REP socket pair + zmq_poll deadline
variants.implementation_notes: The REQ/REP socket types are request-reply built into the transport: a REQ socket sends one request and accepts exactly one reply, which the socket pair routes back, so no application-level correlation table exists. The deadline comes from zmq_poll's millisecond timeout (or ZMQ_RCVTIMEO), and the server's REP socket strictly receives before it sends. Use it when the process can ship libzmq and one request is outstanding per socket; avoid it when requests must be pipelined over shared connections, where an identifier-based design or a ROUTER/DEALER topology is needed instead.
pitfalls: REQ/REP sockets alternate strictly: after a timeout the socket is still in the receive state, so it must be rebuilt (disconnect/reconnect or a fresh socket) or the next send fails.
Polling a REQ socket for a reply that never comes does not cancel the request: the peer may still process it and the reply is dropped when the socket closes.
